# ZCode Functionality and Third-Party Component Notice

> English translation maintained by Gian of the [upstream NOTICE](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/NOTICE.md) at commit `aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f`.
> References below to this repository, application, or project mean upstream ZCode, not Gian. The original upstream document and the production Runtime build are unchanged. Translation changes are recorded separately from the upstream source identity.

This notice applies to the source published in the upstream repository and its build outputs. Features, permissions, storage locations, and network behavior differ between execution modes. The defaults of one mode must not be treated as uniform project-wide settings.

## 1. AI Output, Execution Permissions, and Automation Risks

AI-generated code, commands, explanations, files, and suggestions may contain errors, omissions, security defects, or third-party rights issues. Check actual files, command exit statuses, tool results, and tests. A model's claims that work is complete, safely handled, or authorized do not establish facts or authorization. Review targets, recipients, and effects before important operations, and retain recoverable backups.

File, terminal, Git, Agent tools, and external processes can read and write files, start processes, and access networks within the permissions of the operating-system account running them. In Web or remote workspaces, execution may occur on a server, SSH host, WSL, or container, not the device displaying the page. The shared Agent execution adapter does not provide an operating-system sandbox by default. Working directories, workspace identities, Git worktrees, browser-page isolation, and Node REPL contexts are not system-level isolation guarantees for every tool.

Shared runtime configuration defaults to `build` permission mode. The standalone CLI uses `yolo` for noninteractive `--prompt` tasks when `--mode` is omitted. Interactive, desktop, resumed, and hosted sessions may use their own configured, saved, or supplied modes. Per-operation confirmation depends on tool declarations, permission rules, and execution mode. Without a simultaneous read-only planning restriction, `yolo` permits ordinary tool operations; interactive tools and tools explicitly requiring confirmation retain their own rules. Model tool approval is not a single permission switch for the whole application. Terminal operations, plugin processes, and update downloads need not follow that same approval path. See [CLI prompt mode](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/apps/zcode-cli/packages/cli/src/run.ts#L486) and [tool permission decisions](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/apps/zcode-cli/packages/core/src/permission/service.ts#L97).

| Capability or hook | Effects and boundaries |
| --- | --- |
| Files, Git, terminals, Shell, Node REPL | May read, write, or delete data, execute programs, and access networks. Git, package managers, and user commands may trigger their own scripts and hooks. Task snapshots, Git checkpoints, and session recovery do not replace backups of all local files, databases, and external services. |
| User/workspace instructions and skills | Instruction files, skill text, templates, and scripts affect model planning. Reading, installing, or displaying them does not establish trustworthiness, legality, or official security review. |
| Lifecycle hooks | `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, and `Stop` can run commands or processes. Inputs may include prompts, working paths, tool arguments, results, and responses. Hooks may add context, rewrite tool input, or participate in permission decisions. |
| Workspace-hook trust | Workspace hooks are reviewed against workspace identity and declaration digests. Declaration changes invalidate earlier trust. This is not uniform review of plugin hooks, MCP configuration, or other project scripts. |
| Plugins and MCP | Enabled plugins may introduce automatically executed hooks, local programs, and remote tools. The Agent runtime configuration includes workspace MCP in automatic connection scope. When MCP is enabled and the runtime starts, configured commands, environment variables, authentication headers, or OAuth may connect to services. Plugin hooks and workspace hooks use different admission paths. |
| Startup and installation scripts | Desktop or terminal environment discovery may execute a login shell and its startup configuration. Dependency installation may run lifecycle scripts such as native-module builds. These can precede model tasks and are not necessarily commands individually approved through the model. |
| Subagents, workflows, and background tasks | May continue invoking models, running commands, and incurring costs or external side effects. Stopping a session, changing pages, or cancelling a request cannot reverse completed writes, publication, uploads, or other external actions. |
| Desktop scheduled and idle tasks | May execute from saved configuration while the scheduler and execution host are available, including when the window is hidden. Closing a window may only hide it to the background or tray. Explicit quit, sleep, disconnection, and account/model availability affect execution. There is no guarantee of running while powered off or catching up every missed task. Including a Cron tool does not give the standalone CLI a persistent scheduler service. |
| Embedded browser and Browser Use | May visit pages, read content, capture screenshots or recordings, click, type, upload, and download. Imported or reused browser login state may enable access to private data, form submission, or remote account changes. Visiting pages communicates with the sites and their loaded services. |
| Computer Use | The included Computer Use package is an unavailable placeholder. Calls return an unavailable error; it does not provide system screenshots or system control. See the [Computer Use entry](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/packages/zcode-cua/index.js#L3). |
| Web services and remote environments | Reachability, login authentication, process accounts, and file permissions depend on deployment. Authentication defaults differ by entrypoint and listening address. Loopback listening, origin checks, and SSH tunnels enforce different boundaries; a development service or local core port is not automatically suitable for public exposure. |
| Content sharing, import, and previews | May read or transmit conversations, code, attachments, and generated material. Shared context, pages, and imported files are external input. A ZCode-branded link does not establish trust or copyright permission for its contents. |

Pages, repositories, tool output, and third-party instructions may attempt to induce additional actions. Limit operating-system accounts, credentials, and network permissions when handling untrusted projects, and review sensitive operations.

Self-hosted Web and remote services require authentication, transport protection, and access control appropriate to the actual entrypoint. Application login is not a substitute for deployment security. See the upstream [README](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/README.md) for Web startup and authentication. The standalone remote service core accepts only loopback listening and does not provide equivalent external account authentication. HTTP/WS and HTTPS/WSS or SSH offer different protections. Not all deployments are encrypted by default, and remote hosts or service operators may be able to access processed data. See [listening restrictions](https://github.com/zai-org/ZCode/blob/aac4755666d09fdcd70272fcf063c077a639015f/packages/zcode-server-cli/src/server-core/http.ts#L115).

## 2. Upload Interfaces, Outbound Requests, and Business Uses

| Scenario | Purpose, triggers, and data scope |
| --- | --- |
| Model and auxiliary-model requests | Task execution, compaction, titles, memory, historical-session extraction, goal-completion verification, AI Git commit messages, and model connectivity tests may invoke models; some auxiliary requests run automatically with a task. Relevant prompts, history, code, diffs, tool results, or attachments are sent according to the feature. Connectivity tests use fixed probe messages. Requests may include authentication and client, session, request, or trace identifiers. Anthropic-compatible calls append device and session identifiers. Recipients depend on the actual endpoint, gateway forwarding below, and proxy configuration, not merely the SDK name. |
| Login, authorization, accounts, and API credentials | Login, authorization-code exchange, login polling, and account/entitlement queries may send authorization state, codes, access tokens, polling credentials, and client identifiers. Login or account resolution may automatically query, retrieve, or create project API keys. Pricing refresh may create missing keys for subscribed team projects. Embedded plan pages may receive login credentials, language, theme, device/account identifiers, and application version after origin checks. The built-in account adapter currently does not implement account refresh-token exchange; MCP OAuth refresh is separate. Account authentication establishes identity, not individual confirmation for every later transmission. External authorization pages' internal handling has not been verified in this repository. |
| Plans, orders, payments, and quotas | Quota resets and related synchronization may send account credentials, personal/team/project scope, reset types, and idempotency identifiers. Opportunity requests, status polling, and read acknowledgments may run automatically. Registered order estimation/creation/cancellation, renewals, payment methods, and payment services may transmit products, order/payment/authorization identifiers, amounts, subscription choices, and caller-supplied channel/trace fields. A service method does not imply every distribution has a purchasing UI or that opening a page initiates payment. |
| Official Coding Plan model gateway forwarding | The code matches two listed official Anthropic-compatible model endpoints by protocol, host, effective port, and path. Matches are automatically forwarded to the ZCode gateway, preserving method, body, query parameters, and all request headers except Host, including authentication. `ZCODE_BASE_URL` or `ZCODE_ENDPOINT_ORIGIN` may change the gateway origin. Forwarding has no additional per-request confirmation. Matching depends on the URL; a user-created provider does not necessarily bypass it. Gateway-side handling is outside the verified client-source scope. |
| Providers, business configuration, and connectivity checks | Background startup checks, configuration refresh, service checks, or page activity may access provider catalogs, business configuration, help content, and CDNs. They may send URLs, versions, platforms, and interface-specific origin information. Help requests may include device identifiers, and connectivity checks may include configured authentication headers. Provider catalog downloads and public configuration reads do not inherit control-plane authentication. Some requests operate independently of model tasks and manual refresh. Model connectivity tests use the model-request path. A service method's existence does not imply every check runs at startup. |
| Search, page processing, and remote resources | Model tools, page visits, and resource rendering may send queries, URLs, headers, and normal network information to model providers, target websites, or resource services. WebSearch currently uses model providers with native search. WebFetch content may subsequently be sent to a model with processing instructions; downloading a page does not imply subsequent local-only handling. Websites, marketplace images, and other resources expose requests and IP information to recipients. |
| MCP connections, OAuth, and tool calls | When enabled MCP configuration is loaded, workspace or plugin services may connect automatically, negotiate protocols, and discover tools. OAuth may perform discovery, client registration, authorization exchange, and automatic token refresh. Tool calls send arguments and may append absolute workspace paths, workspace identity, session/turn/trace identifiers, and remote session identifiers. HTTP/SSE sends to configured services; stdio first reaches a local or execution-host process whose later network behavior depends on that program. Tool approval does not uniformly cover connection, discovery, or refresh. |
| SSH, WSL, containers, and other execution environments | Connections and task execution may transfer protocol commands, prompts, files, attachments, tool results, and terminal state across environments. Personal provider configuration, selected accounts, and credentials allowed for synchronization, including account API keys and OAuth access/refresh tokens, may be transferred automatically when an environment first connects and when related configuration or credentials change during the connection. This has no separate item-by-item credential confirmation. SSH may involve network transport; WSL/containers may use file copies or process input. These transfers are not necessarily to an official cloud. |
| Skills, MCP, plugins, and configuration synchronization | Selection and synchronization in settings may transfer skill/plugin directories, support files, marketplace sources, and configuration to a target environment. Callers may also invoke service interfaces directly. Skill synchronization may include files inside selected directories. MCP configuration may contain arguments, environment variables, headers, authentication, and local paths. Sensitive-field filtering for some plugin options is not comprehensive secret detection for directory archives or all configuration. |
| Attachments and media previews | Files, images, or text may come from selection, drag-and-drop, paste, or task output. Once an attachment is in the input area with an execution session, pre-transfer may start before Send is clicked; restored sessions may continue queued transfers. Local paths may be referenced without upload. Protocol chunk uploads and remote pre-transfers target the execution host. Remote previews may read media back from that host. Local or cross-environment processing is not public publication, but content may later enter model or sharing paths. |
| Session sharing, browsing, and import | Sharing may submit public projections of selected session rows and materializable attachments, including user text, model responses and reasoning, tool input/output, and metadata. Selection may first query sharing capabilities without sending session projection contents. Normal UI publication requires disclosure confirmation; the service validates a caller-supplied confirmation time before preparing a share, uploading attachments, and committing publication. Attachments may therefore be sent before final publication succeeds, but preparation/upload follows that disclosure check. The UI currently defaults to publicly importable sharing; browsing/import does not depend on the publication checkbox. A confirmation timestamp does not prove every caller used the UI checkbox. Browsing/import sends share codes and available authentication and accesses attachment URLs; import also sends a request identifier. Projection filtering and text processing are not comprehensive secret detection. Local deletion or cancellation does not guarantee deletion of external uploads or recipients' copies. |
| Idle-task tickets and status synchronization | Availability checks, ticket queues, status synchronization, and redemption send task/ticket/source/request identifiers, Coding Plan identity, and authentication. Pending tickets can trigger continuing background requests. These requests are not full task prompts; model content travels through its separate path. |
| Feedback, follow-up messages, and diagnostic attachments | Submitted feedback may send text, contact information, account/client information, screenshots, and filenames. The service supports follow-up messages and attachments, and background jobs report upload results; an endpoint does not imply a current UI editing entrypoint. After ticket creation the form may close while selected screenshots and logs continue uploading. Exiting before creation requests cancellation. Attachments first obtain upload credentials from the feedback service, then upload directly to returned object-storage addresses. Desktop logs are unchecked by default. If selected, files are chosen by local modification date and archive rules and processed in full, not necessarily only today's entries. Omitting logs does not suppress text or other attachments. Text processing does not guarantee screenshots or arbitrary files are redacted. |
| Mobile remote control | After enabling and pairing remote control, desktop and mobile Web exchange session content, input, task status, permission requests, and attachment-preview messages through an external relay. The relay handles authentication, pairing, heartbeats, and forwarding, not task execution. Pairing and connections send device, window, and session identifiers. The relay address follows distribution configuration and may be overridden by `ZCODE_WEB_REMOTE_CONTROL_RELAY_WS_URL`. |
| Third-party chat Bots | Configured platforms, such as Telegram or Feishu/Lark, can drive tasks through incoming messages. Depending on reply mode, Bots send assistant responses, tool calls, file-change summaries, and permission requests to the platform, whose operator can access that content. Bot credentials are stored in the local credential service; configuration stores references only. |
| Marketing and rewards | After login, business services may supply banner/popup configuration and resource packages. Clicks and dismissals report confirmation/cancellation events; claim operations invoke plan-claim interfaces. The rewards center opens in an embedded page whose bridge receives theme, language, and login state. |
| Installation, plugin acquisition, remote deployment, and updates | Installation, discovery, authentication, deployment, and updates access repositories, package services, marketplaces, CDNs, or update servers. The unified CLI installer reads version manifests and downloads releases from configured distribution sources. Desktop automatic updates depend on distribution and runtime conditions. When enabled, startup and periodic checks may send platform, channel, and device information; platform may distinguish architecture, and versions affect update selection. Open-source builds disable automatic updates by default as a build-time option. When enabled, development and packaged builds accept `ZCODE_UPDATE_FEED_URL` and `--zcode-update-feed-url` overrides for diagnosis and emergencies. Downloaded code may later be installed or executed. Remote deployment may upload/copy existing or downloaded components to target environments. Checking, installation, and execution have different controls and do not uniformly prompt before every step. |
| Delivery/publication by tools, hooks, workflows, and automatic tasks | Shell, terminal, Git, Node REPL, browser, plugin, MCP, and workflow operations may read task data, upload files/output, and alter external services. Lifecycle hooks and configured scheduled/background tasks may run programs. Permission rules, modes, plugin configuration, and system accounts determine execution scope. Not every outbound item is individually selected or separately confirmed. Local cancellation or undo may not restore external state after publication, sending, purchasing, or deployment. See the permission boundaries above and in this section. |
| Development tests, debugging, and request recording | Explicit developer tools may send test prompts, samples, and authentication headers to configured real model/tool services. Recording proxies configured for real upstreams may forward requests; test/recording names do not imply offline operation. Request traces and debug files may store model content locally. These entrypoints differ from ordinary product execution. |
| Builds, signing, and maintainer publication | Explicit install/build/release scripts may download dependencies, native binaries, and runtimes, copy build material to release shares, push Git, or submit material to signing tools and Apple notarization. External signing tools and separately configured CI/storage/distribution services have their own network behavior. Unexamined flows cannot be considered verified merely from script names. Entrypoints, environments, and credential requirements differ. CLI SEA shared-directory publication/upload validates third-party notice material first and stops if validation fails. Native-search preparation currently verifies and extracts repository-bundled archives for the target platform rather than downloading them at that step; other components such as Node have separate download paths. |

These purposes describe interfaces provided by upstream ZCode. User-authored scripts, arbitrary configured endpoints, and separately installed third-party components may send additional data. Being launched through ZCode does not establish official review of their purposes or recipients.

## 3. Local Data, Logs, and Credentials

Data may reside on the desktop, in browsers, on CLI hosts, in SSH/WSL environments, and in external services. Desktop/server data locations depend on runtime and startup configuration and may include settings, sessions, attachments, caches, task records, plugins, and logs. The standalone CLI session database defaults to `~/.zcode/cli/db/db.sqlite`. Closing windows, logging out, uninstalling, or deleting one workspace does not establish that every copy in other environments, independent data directories, backups, or external services has been removed.

Memory defaults and entrypoints differ: standalone CLI configuration enables memory by default, while desktop settings disable it. Enabled memory may analyze saved sessions, persist results, and reuse them in later tasks. Extraction and organization may cause additional model requests. Automation schedules, run records, and unfinished tasks have their own persistence; restoring those records does not reverse earlier external actions or guarantee complete replay.

Shared Agent model-input/output logging is enabled locally by default in development and production, except in tests. Logs may contain prompts, code, context, tool arguments, and model responses. Headers and some image/video data are redacted, but not all user text is necessarily redacted. Production defaults include rotation/trimming; explicitly enabling full retention changes that behavior. Desktop main processes, Hosts, schedulers, Web services, and remote daemons also keep their own logs/crash records. One log limit is not a project-wide retention policy.

Credential storage differs by component. CLI shared credential files use encryption whose default key may be derived from local environment information; readers also accept plaintext records. Desktop/Node services likewise use encrypted local files with configurable or environment-derived keys, not the system keychain. Web OAuth credentials may be stored in localStorage. Model configuration, environment variables, plugin/MCP settings, SSH configuration, and synchronized remote data may contain valid credentials. These stores are not uniformly system keychains, hardware isolation, or guarantees that credentials never leave the machine.

The embedded browser persists browsing data. Explicitly importing another browser's Cookies and LocalStorage can import its login state. Clearing cache differs from clearing all site data. Browser records, downloads, page recordings, and model logs need not share a cleanup entrypoint. Do not commit real keys or tokens. Before copying logs, submitting feedback, sharing conversations, or backing up data directories, review the recipients and scope so real credentials, raw sessions, and private project content are not submitted to public repositories or issue reports.
